target: Systems / quant-developer / low-latency C++ internships (HFT firms, trading-systems teams), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Designed the order book with std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map and an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1), which ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec and hit a 1.2 µs p99 on a separate 2M-event run
bullet_feedback.problem: The p99 does not say what it is the 99th percentile of (per-message processing in the book? per add/cancel/execute? including parsing?), and the bullet switches units from 'messages' (bullet 1: 50.9M messages) to 'events' (here: 1.26M events/sec) without saying whether they are the same thing. It also does not say whether these numbers were taken before or after the core-pinning fix described in bullet 4.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A low-latency reader's first question is 'p99 of what, measured where, on which setup'. 1.26M/sec implies a ~0.8 µs mean per event, so a 1.2 µs p99 is plausible only if both cover the same unit of work; if the reader can't confirm that, the two numbers look like they came from different benchmarks stitched together.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what operation the 1.2 µs p99 times (and whether it includes feed parsing); whether 'events' = the IEX messages from bullet 1; whether the runs were core-pinned
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name the timed operation next to the percentile and use one noun (messages or events) across bullets 1-2, e.g. '...1.2 µs p99 per-message book update on a separate 2M-message run'. If the runs were pinned, a two-word 'pinned core' tag removes the ambiguity with bullet 4.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine’s event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk
bullet_feedback.problem: Only the read-side results are reported; write/ingest throughput, which is the LSM tree's main reason to exist and the dominant operation for an append-heavy event log, is absent, and the workload mix ('identical 2M-record workloads') is not described.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A storage-literate reader sees a comparison that reports only the dimensions where the B+ tree wins and suspects cherry-picking or a read-heavy workload that was never stated. It also invites 'why would you put an event log in a B+ tree?', which the bullet doesn't answer.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: read/write mix of the workload; whether write throughput was measured and how the two compared
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: State the workload shape in a few words before the result (e.g. 'on identical read-heavy 2M-record workloads') or, if write numbers exist, give the trade-off in both directions instead of '27% more disk' alone.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Traced an apparent 1.65x regression to the CPU frequency governor with perf counters and a do-nothing control book to rule out a code change, which led to core pinning that cut run-to-run variance from 6% to 0.06%
bullet_feedback.problem: 'run-to-run variance from 6% to 0.06%' does not say which metric varied (throughput? p99?), how it is computed (coefficient of variation? max-min spread?), or over how many runs. The cause is the frequency governor but the fix named is core pinning; a reader expects the governor to be fixed (performance mode / fixed frequency) and wonders whether pinning alone explains a 100x drop.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A 100x variance reduction is the most striking number on the page and the easiest to challenge; without the metric and run count it reads as a possibly lucky small sample. The cause/fix mismatch makes the diagnosis look less rigorous than the control-book method suggests.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which measurement's variance, how computed, number of runs; whether the governor was also set as part of the fix
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name the measured quantity and run count in place of the bare word 'variance' (e.g. 'cut throughput spread across N runs from 6% to 0.06%'), and make the fix match the cause ('...led to pinning cores and [the governor change, if one was made]').

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built a C++17 order book and matching engine to replay 50.9M real IEX exchange messages without ever resyncing, which agreed with the exchange on 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices
bullet_feedback.problem: The single mismatched fill is reported but not explained, and '100% of top-of-book prices' does not say how often top of book was compared (every message? every BBO update?).
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the strongest correctness claim on the page and an HFT interviewer will ask about the one miss immediately; that's fine if the candidate knows, but the page gives no hint the miss was investigated.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify (for the interview, not necessarily the page): cause of the 1 mismatched fill; granularity of the top-of-book comparison
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep as is unless space allows a short '(checked at every BBO update)'-style qualifier; be ready to explain the one miss.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting a Claude skill into focused sub-skills that call Python search and validation tools instead of relying on open-ended model search
bullet_feedback.problem: 'under 15s' does not say whether it is a typical, average, or worst-case generation time, or over how many requests; for this persona every latency should name its statistic. The bold on '65%' pulls the eye to a non-domain metric.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The trading-firm reader discounts latency claims without a stated statistic, and the bolded 65% competes with the order-book numbers that should own the skim.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether 'under 15s' is median, mean, or max
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Add the statistic in one word ('median generation time ...') and drop the bold here so bold stays on the C++ project.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
bullet_feedback.problem: 'end-to-end latency 34%' does not say per-document or whole-batch, nor mean vs a percentile, and gives no baseline magnitude.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: For this reader a latency percentage with no unit and no statistic is unverifiable; it signals the candidate's measurement discipline outside the C++ project is looser.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: per-document or per-batch latency; mean or percentile
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name what is timed ('per-document end-to-end latency') and the statistic; consider removing the bold on 34% for the same reason as above.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga’s Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
bullet_feedback.problem: 'Tortuga' is undefined (product name? company?), and 'to reduce database load and latency' states an intent with no result.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A reader can't tell what Tortuga is and the bullet ends on an aim rather than an outcome, so it reads as filler next to the measured project bullets.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what Tortuga is; whether any load or latency change was observed
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Introduce Tortuga in two words where it first appears (e.g. 'our class scheduler, Tortuga') and either state an observed effect or rephrase the ending so it doesn't promise a result it doesn't give.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline for a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick grasps that avoid hitting the table
bullet_feedback.problem: No outcome, and the content (prompt-tuning, VLM grasp selection) is unrelated to low-latency systems; it takes two lines of a page whose strength is the C++ project.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: For a trading-systems screen this bullet adds breadth but no hiring signal; it is low cost but dilutes the systems story.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Acceptable to keep; if space is needed for clarifications in the project bullets, this is the first candidate to shorten to one line.

page_feedback.problem: All low-latency/C++ evidence lives in one two-month side project; every Experience entry is cloud, Java, or LLM work, and there is no evidence of concurrency, threading, memory layout/allocation, or networking anywhere on the page.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: An HFT screener will read this as 'strong cloud/AI intern with one excellent C++ project' rather than 'systems engineer who repeatedly builds performance-sensitive software', which is the intended profile. The project carries the whole application.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the project first (correct choice). If any experience bullet involved real performance trade-offs, lead with the performance mechanism rather than the AI/cloud framing; otherwise accept the gap and be ready to discuss threading/cache behavior of the engine in interviews.

page_feedback.problem: Project dates (Jul 2026 – Aug 2026) overlap completely with the Capital One internship (Jun 2026 – Aug 2026).
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A 50.9M-message replay engine with two storage backends and a perf investigation built during a full-time internship invites a 'how much of this did you actually do?' question.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: No change required; be ready to explain the timeline. If the work started earlier, the dates could reflect that.

page_feedback.problem: Bold is applied to 65% (Capital One) and 34% (Amazon Leo) as well as to the order-book numbers, giving five bold anchors of equal weight.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The skim splits attention between AI-workflow percentages and the C++ throughput numbers this target hires on.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Limit bold to the project's numbers (e.g. 50.9M, 1.26M events/sec, the p99) so the 7-second read lands on the systems story.

page_feedback.problem: Roughly the bottom sixth of the page is empty while several project bullets need a few more words to define their measurements.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The clarifications requested above (what the p99 times, workload mix, variance metric) can be added without crowding the page.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Spend the slack on the project bullets' measurement qualifiers rather than on new content.

page_feedback.problem: Skills lists C and Rust, and generic entries 'data structures and algorithms, benchmarking', none of which are backed by a bullet.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A systems interviewer may probe Rust or C directly; generic entries read as filler.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep only languages you are comfortable being quizzed on; consider dropping the generic 'data structures and algorithms' phrase.

keep: IEX Order Book & Matching Engine project placed first, above Experience
The fill-level correctness check against the exchange ('agreed with the exchange on 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices')
The use of a do-nothing control book and perf counters to rule out a code change in the regression bullet
Reporting a p99 rather than only a mean, and stating that it came from a separate 2M-event run
